parole.significato: A strict Anabaptist sect living mainly in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Indiana.
parole.testo: From Pennsylvania German Amisch or German Amische, after the name of the Swiss preacher Jakob Amman (1645-1730). The surname is a contraction of Old High German ambahtman.

parole.significato: Familiar term of address for a boy; bub; bubba.
parole.testo: Perhaps from brother, as pronounced by young children who are not yet able to properly pronounce its complex consonants, but alternatively perhaps from Pennsylvania German; see bub. Compare sissy.

parole.significato: A stylized goldfinch in Pennsylvania Dutch folk art, representing happiness and good fortune.
parole.testo: From Pennsylvania German distelfink, homologous to High German Distelfink (“thistle finch”), the European goldfinch.

parole.significato: Lacking dexterity; not skilled; clumsy.
parole.testo: Originated in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, from the older form doppich, from Pennsylvania German doppich, related to German täppisch (“clumsy”).

parole.significato: Clumsy; lacking dexterity; not skilled.
parole.testo: Originated in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, from Pennsylvania German doppich (“clumsy”), related to German täppisch (“clumsy”).

parole.significato: To submerge briefly in a liquid.
parole.testo: From Pennsylvania German dunke, from Middle High German dunken, from Old High German dunkōn (“to dip, submerge, dunk”), from Proto-West Germanic *þunkōn (“to make wet”), possibly from Proto-Germanic *þunkōną, from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to moisten, wet”). Cognate with German tunken (“to dunk”)

parole.significato: To confuse or puzzle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Pennsylvania German verhuddle.

parole.significato: An event where Pennsylvania German language and culture is celebrated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Pennsylvania German Versammling/Fersommling.

parole.significato: A groundhog, a woodchuck.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Pennsylvania German Grundsow/Grundsau (literally “ground sow”) which is itself a calque of English groundhog.

parole.significato: To cast a spell on (specifically an evil spell), to bewitch.
parole.testo: First attested about 1830, from Pennsylvania German hexe (“to practice witchcraft”), from German hexen (compare Hexe (“witch”)). The noun appeared later, in the 1850s. parole.significato: A hex sign on Pennsylvanian barns to scare away evil spirits or simply for decoration.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Pennsylvania German Hexefuss, literally "witch foot". See Hexe, Fuss for more.

parole.significato: witchcraft
parole.testo: Borrowed from Pennsylvania German Hexerei.

parole.testo: Borrowed in a modified form from Pennsylvania German Christ-kinkle, from German Christkindl (“(dialectal diminutive) Christ Child”), Christkind (“Christ Child”), from Christ (“Christ”) + Kindl (dialectal diminutive), Kind (“child”).

parole.significato: Synonym of scrapple (“dish of pork scraps”).
parole.testo: From Pennsylvania German Pannhaas.

parole.significato: A decoration or ornament in the Nativity tradition, usually placed under a Christmas tree.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Pennsylvania German Putz; compare German Putz (“ornament, decoration, finery”), putzen (“to clean; decorate”). Compare the above.

parole.significato: A kind of small dumpling made from egg and wheat flour, often eaten in soup, especially among the Pennsylvania Dutch an…
parole.testo: Probably from (Pennsylvania German, from) Palatine Rhine Franconian Riwwel, Ribbel, Riebel (compare Volga German Rievel, Ribel, Riebel).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Pennsylvania German rumspringe (“to jump around”). Compare German rumspringen.

parole.significato: A large highly decorative German/Dutch-style piece of furniture, which combines aspects of a clothing wardrobe, curio,…
parole.testo: From Pennsylvania German; cognate to German Schrank.

parole.significato: Cottage cheese.
parole.testo: In Pennsylvanian usage, borrowed from Pennsylvania German Schmierkaes. (In Texas, presumably from the cognate equivalent in Texas German.) Compare schmear, from Yiddish.

parole.significato: In American folklore, a dragon-like beast said to inhabit central Maryland and neighbouring regions.
parole.testo: Probably a modification of Pennsylvania German schnelle Geeschter (“quick ghosts”).

parole.significato: A child, especially a mischievous one; especially as a nickname or term of endearment, or exasperation. Alternative let…
parole.testo: From German or Pennsylvania German, related to German Schnickschnack (“chatter”) (see schnacken, *schnicken) + -el + Fritz (a nickname derived from Friedrich), thus probably originally denoting someone chatty or impulsive.

parole.significato: A shrewd person not guided by principles, especially a politician.
parole.testo: 19th-century American English. Possibly from snallygaster, a mythical beast that preys on poultry and children; possibly from Pennsylvania German schnelle geeschter, from German schnell (“quick”) + Geist (“spirit”).
